meta.title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

exploratory.title: Heterogeneity by respondent ideology
exploratory.rationale: Tests whether the negative effect of misinformation/fact-check on sharing is stronger among conservative respondents, who may be more receptive to partisan misinformation.
exploratory.method: IPW-weighted OLS (HC2) with arm_code × is_conservative interaction, same covariates as registered H1 model, restricted to respondents with non-missing ideo5_self (n=9,910).
exploratory.finding: The negative effect of both misinformation and fact-check on sharing is significantly weaker among conservative respondents (interaction: Misinfo +0.104, p=0.001; Fact-check +0.112, p<0.001), meaning conservatives are less deterred from sharing by either information type.

exploratory.title: Treatment effect stability across conjoint trials
exploratory.rationale: Verifies that the treatment effect is stable across the four conjoint trials, ruling out order effects or respondent fatigue as alternative explanations for the registered estimates.
exploratory.method: Re-fit the registered H1 model (arm_code Treatment coding, IPW, HC2, same covariates) separately on each of the four trials (n≈2,972 per trial).
exploratory.finding: The misinformation effect declines modestly from −0.200 in trial 1 to −0.140 in trial 4, suggesting a mild fatigue/order effect, but the effect remains large and significant in every trial.

exploratory.title: Treatment effect by headline theme
exploratory.rationale: Tests whether the negative effect is concentrated in specific topic areas, which would suggest the result is content-dependent rather than a general response to information type.
exploratory.method: Re-fit the registered H1 model separately for each of 15 headline themes (n≥100 per theme), extracting arm-specific estimates.
exploratory.finding: The misinformation effect varies substantially by theme (range −0.325 to +0.152), with some topics showing a positive effect, indicating the overall negative result is driven by a subset of themes rather than being uniform across content.

lit.text: The retrieved literature offers only limited direct coverage of the study's hypotheses. Lazer et al. (2018) frame fake news as a multidisciplinary problem, noting that the type and source of information shape how audiences evaluate its credibility, which is broadly consistent with H1 and H2. Gigerenzer and Gaissmaier (2010) describe heuristics as efficient processes that ignore part of the available information, providing a mechanism by which information type could influence plausibility judgments (H2). Beyond these, the remaining works address topics (tourism climate, energy acceptance, immigration prejudice, brand psychology, etc.) that do not speak directly to information-type effects on sharing or plausibility.

takeaways: Misinformation headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than True/neutral (placebo) headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), a registered test on the forced-choice sharing outcome.
Fact-check headlines were chosen for sharing 13.3 points less often than True/neutral headlines (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]), so both information types lowered the sharing choice.
Misinformation was chosen as more plausible 18.6 points less often than True/neutral (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4]); Fact-check was 12.4 points lower (95% CI [−14.7, −10.2]).
Exploratory, unreviewed checks suggest the sharing effects vary by respondent ideology and headline theme, so the average effects should not be read as uniform.
Both registered hypotheses carry an undocumented deviation, and the estimates come from a single survey, so treat the exact magnitudes with caution.
sections.abstract: Does the type of information in a headline change whether people choose to share it and whether they judge it more plausible? We analyse a US conjoint experiment on a YouGov sample (12,000 responses) in which respondents made binary forced choices between headlines. Headlines were Misinformation, Fact-check, or True/neutral (placebo, the reference). Relative to True/neutral, Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 percentage points less often (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and Fact-check 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility choices followed the same pattern: Misinformation was 18.6 points lower (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4]) and Fact-check 12.4 points lower (95% CI [−14.7, −10.2]). All four tests were two-sided with p<0.001. Both hypotheses carry an undocumented deviation from the registered plan, and the choice format may not reflect real-world sharing, so magnitudes should be read cautiously.
sections.design_notes: The study is registered (AsPredicted #132508), but both hypotheses carry a deviation tag with no documentation of what changed, so readers should weigh the results accordingly. The raw and eligible sample is 12,000 responses; the sharing model uses 11,882 and the plausibility model 11,884 after dropping rows with missing values. The True/neutral (placebo) control has 4,145 responses. Outcomes are binary forced choices, and standard errors are clustered. Effects are percentage-point differences from the control.

results.H1: Both treatment arms lowered the chance that a headline was chosen for sharing. Misinformation was 18.2 points lower than True/neutral (−0.182; 95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]; two-sided p<0.001), from 60.3% to 42.1%. Fact-check was 13.3 points lower (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]; p<0.001), at 47.0%. The intervals are tight and clear of zero. Because the deviation from the plan is undocumented, its effect on these estimates is unknown.
results.H2: Plausibility choices showed the same pattern. Misinformation was chosen as more plausible 18.6 points less often than True/neutral (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4]; two-sided p<0.001), from 60.1% to 41.6%. Fact-check was 12.4 points lower (95% CI [−14.7, −10.2]; p<0.001). Misinformation's drop is larger than Fact-check's, though the intervals for the two arms are close. The undocumented deviation applies here as well.

exploratory.E1: In an unreviewed check, the negative effects on sharing were weaker among more conservative respondents. The interaction was +0.104 for Misinformation (95% CI [0.041, 0.166]) and +0.112 for Fact-check (95% CI [0.050, 0.173]).
exploratory.E2: An unreviewed check by trial found the Misinformation effect shrinking from −0.200 in trial 1 to −0.140 in trial 4. Estimates stayed clearly negative in every trial, and Fact-check showed a similar shrinkage.
exploratory.E3: An unreviewed check by headline theme found large variation in the Misinformation effect, from −0.325 for one theme to nearly zero for others. Some themes had intervals including zero, so the average may hide uneven effects.

sections.limitations: Both hypotheses carry deviation tags with no documentation, so we cannot say how the analysis differs from the registered plan. The outcomes are forced choices between headlines, which may not match real sharing behaviour on social platforms. Only two treatment arms are compared to one control, and the arms and the plausibility and sharing outcomes are tested without correction for multiple comparisons, although the effects are far from the threshold. The exploratory analyses come from unreviewed code and are cut into smaller subgroups, so they are best treated as leads for follow-up rather than findings.
